entries.answer: Tell me the exact iPhone or iPad model and iOS version. Franklin can compare that model with the same hardware catalog used by the site's Compatibility checker rather than guessing from the product family.
The current compatibility policy places A11 below the normal GPU floor. Treat iPhone X-class A11 hardware as unsupported for the normal path rather than expecting settings tweaks to fix it.

A12 is an experimental path in the current compatibility policy. It uses the lowest route and should not be treated as equivalent to the normal A13 baseline. Stability and feature coverage can be limited.
A13 is the normal supported GPU baseline in the current compatibility policy. Memory is still important: iPhone 11-family devices have limited headroom compared with newer 6 GB or 8 GB models.
A14 is on the normal supported path and enables effects the policy omits on A13. The exact iPhone 12 model still matters because RAM differs between standard and Pro models.
A15 is supported, but the project distinguishes GPU classes and memory capacity. A 4 GB A15 device still needs more conservative memory settings than a 6 GB A15 model.

A16 sits above the A13 baseline and is in the supported class. On 6 GB devices, High textures can be reasonable when the app-memory allowance supports that tier, but stability matters more than maxing every option.

entries.answer: A17 Pro is in the higher GPU class and iPhone 15 Pro models have much more memory headroom than 4 GB devices. That improves options, but it still does not guarantee a fixed FPS in every scene.
A18-family hardware is in the higher compatibility class. Use the device checker for the exact model because thermals, GPU class, and memory still determine the practical settings.

3 GB is below the project's practical 4 GB RAM minimum in the current compatibility policy. Increased Memory Limit cannot create physical RAM, so this should not be treated as a normal supported configuration.
4 GB falls inside the project's automatic low-memory range. Use Normal textures, conservative resolution, keep expensive effects limited, and preserve Increased Memory Limit when eligible.
6 GB gives noticeably more headroom than 4 GB. The policy maps it to a higher memory tier, but the effective tier can still be reduced by the actual app-memory allowance.
8 GB provides strong physical-memory headroom for this project. The policy can allow a Very High texture tier when the app-memory allowance also supports it, but thermal and GPU limits still matter.

The native port combines physical RAM with the app-memory allowance and uses the lower effective tier. A phone can have plenty of physical RAM and still be limited if the signed app receives a smaller memory allowance.

iRAM+ is the community path for eligible sideloaded apps that need the Increased Memory Limit entitlement. It does not add physical RAM and it cannot make unsupported hardware equivalent to a newer device.
The audited GTA5 build declares iOS 16.3 as its MinimumOSVersion. The site compatibility policy recommends iOS 18 or newer for the current community setup path.
More than 30 GB free is the preferred working headroom in the compatibility policy. 21 to 30 GB is limited, while 20 GB or less is treated as insufficient for a comfortable install/update workflow.
Start by lowering render resolution, not by changing ten options at once. Then keep MSAA off, reduce shadows, use an appropriate texture tier, and choose a stable FPS cap while checking heat.

Stutter can come from asset streaming, memory pressure, shader work, or thermal throttling. Note whether it happens only when moving quickly through the map, only after several minutes, or immediately from launch.

If performance drops after the phone gets hot, thermal throttling is a strong possibility. Lower resolution or FPS cap, avoid charging while testing if practical, remove unnecessary background load, and compare performance from a cool start.

A native open-world game can keep CPU and GPU load high, so battery drain is expected to rise with resolution, frame rate, and graphics effects. A lower FPS cap and render resolution usually reduce power demand.
A stable 30 FPS cap can be better than an unstable higher target on devices with limited thermal or memory headroom. Judge it by frame-time consistency and heat, not just the peak number.
Use 40 FPS only if your device can hold it without repeated thermal drops or heavy stutter. If it oscillates badly, a lower stable cap is usually smoother.
There is no guaranteed 60 FPS target for every device or scene. Resolution, graphics settings, game area, heat, memory pressure, and the current build all affect performance.
Render resolution is one of the strongest performance controls. Start lower on 4 GB or thermally constrained devices, then raise it gradually only after the game is stable.

MetalFX can trade internal render resolution for reconstructed output. It may improve performance, but it also changes memory and rendering cost. Compare it on your actual device rather than assuming it is always faster.
MSAA is expensive on mobile. Keep it off as the default troubleshooting baseline, especially on 4 GB devices or when you are already using a high render resolution.
Shadows can cost both GPU time and memory. Use a modest level first, then raise it only if frame time and thermals remain stable.

Texture quality should follow the effective memory tier. The project policy recommends Normal for the lowest tier, High for the 6 GB-class tier, and Very High only when both physical and app-memory headroom support it.

If performance starts well and degrades after several minutes, compare device temperature and memory behavior. That pattern is more consistent with thermal or accumulated pressure than with a simple unsupported setting.
Stutter that appears mainly while driving quickly can be asset-streaming pressure. Lower texture or resolution pressure first and compare the same route from a fresh launch.

External cooling can change thermal behavior, but it is not a substitute for a stable configuration. First establish a baseline without overheating, then use cooling only as an optional way to sustain performance.
Charging can add heat while the game is already stressing the device. If you are diagnosing thermal drops, compare a cool unplugged test with the same scene before changing graphics settings.
